title: Contracts Act 1950, s 24: when the object or consideration of an agreement is unlawful
citation: Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136), s 24
plain: A contract is void if what it is for, or what is being paid for, is illegal, fraudulent, harms someone, or goes against public policy. A void agreement cannot be enforced by either side.
text:
## Text

"24. The consideration or object of an agreement is lawful, unless— (a) it is forbidden by a law; (b) it is of such a nature that, if permitted, it would defeat any law; (c) it is fraudulent; (d) it involves or implies injury to the person or property of another; or (e) the court regards it as immoral, or opposed to public policy.

In each of the above cases, the consideration or object of an agreement is said to be unlawful. Every agreement of which the object or consideration is unlawful is void."

## In plain words

A contract is void if what it is for, or what is being paid for, is illegal, fraudulent, harms someone, or goes against public policy. A void agreement cannot be enforced by either side.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

Rarely the main issue, but it is the backstop when a clause asks a party to do something unlawful, for example an NDA term that forbids reporting wrongdoing to a regulator, or a services scope that would breach licensing law. Flag such terms as void or unenforceable rather than merely unfavourable.

title: Contracts Act 1950, s 28: agreements in restraint of trade are void
citation: Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136), s 28
plain: In Malaysia, a promise not to carry on a lawful trade or business is void to the extent it restrains that trade. Unlike Singapore or England, there is no general "it was reasonable" escape: the only exceptions are sale of a business's goodwill and partnerships. Only the restraining part fails; the rest of the contract can survive.
text:
## Text

"28. Every agreement by which anyone is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind, is to that extent void."

"Exception 1—One who sells the goodwill of a business may agree with the buyer to refrain carrying on a similar business, within specified local limits, so long as the buyer, or any person deriving title to the goodwill from him, carries on a like business therein: Provided that such limits appear to the court reasonable, regard being had to the nature of the business."

(Exceptions 2 and 3 cover partners on or before dissolution of a partnership, and during the partnership.)

## In plain words

In Malaysia, a promise not to carry on a lawful trade or business is void to the extent it restrains that trade. Unlike Singapore or England, there is no general "it was reasonable" escape: the only exceptions are sale of a business's goodwill and partnerships. Only the restraining part fails; the rest of the contract can survive.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

Non-compete wording inside an NDA or a vendor agreement under Malaysian law is likely void, but it still deters and costs money to fight, and a foreign governing-law clause may change the answer. Whether a non-solicitation clause counts as a restraint under s 28 is not settled by this text; treat it as a risk to raise rather than assume either way. Watch for a proposed amendment that would introduce a reasonableness test.

title: Contracts Act 1950, s 29: agreements in restraint of legal proceedings are void
citation: Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136), s 29
plain: A contract term that completely stops one side from going to court to enforce its rights, or that shortens the time it has to sue, is void to that extent. Agreeing to send disputes to arbitration is expressly allowed.
text:
## Text

"29. Every agreement, by which any party thereto is restricted absolutely from enforcing his rights under or in respect of any contract, by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals, or which limits the time within which he may thus enforce his rights, is void to that extent."

"Exception 1—This section shall not render illegal a contract by which two or more persons agree that any dispute which may arise between them in respect of any subject or class of subjects shall be referred to arbitration, and that only the amount awarded in the arbitration shall be recoverable in respect of the dispute so referred."

## In plain words

A contract term that completely stops one side from going to court to enforce its rights, or that shortens the time it has to sue, is void to that extent. Agreeing to send disputes to arbitration is expressly allowed.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

Two common vendor terms meet this section. A clause saying "any claim must be brought within 6 months" tries to limit the time to enforce rights, which s 29 makes void. A clause that leaves the customer with no remedy at all for a breach can also be struck down (see my-case-cimb-v-bourke). An arbitration clause (for example AIAC) is fine under Exception 1.

title: Contracts Act 1950, s 30: agreements void for uncertainty
citation: Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136), s 30
plain: If nobody can work out what a promise actually means, and the contract gives no way of working it out, that promise is void. Vague words can leave you with nothing to enforce.
text:
## Text

"30. Agreements, the meaning of which is not certain, or capable of being made certain, are void."

## In plain words

If nobody can work out what a promise actually means, and the contract gives no way of working it out, that promise is void. Vague words can leave you with nothing to enforce.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

Watch scope, service levels and fees described only as "to be agreed", "reasonable efforts as determined by the vendor", or with no measurable standard. A promise you cannot pin down may be unenforceable when you need it; ask for a definition, a schedule or a formula that makes it certain.

title: Contracts Act 1950, s 40: ending a contract when the other side refuses to perform
citation: Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136), s 40
plain: If the other side refuses to do what it promised, or makes itself unable to, you may end the contract, unless you have shown by words or conduct that you are happy for it to carry on.
text:
## Text

"40. When a party to a contract has refused to perform, or disabled himself from performing, his promise in its entirety, the promisee may put an end to the contract, unless he has signified, by words or conduct, his acquiescence in its continuance."

## In plain words

If the other side refuses to do what it promised, or makes itself unable to, you may end the contract, unless you have shown by words or conduct that you are happy for it to carry on.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

This is the general-law right to terminate that sits behind any termination clause. If a vendor stops delivering altogether, the customer can end the contract even if the termination clause is narrow, but continuing to accept and pay for partial service may be read as accepting the contract's continuance. Contract termination rights (notice, cure periods) usually add to this right.

title: Contracts Act 1950, s 74: compensation for loss caused by breach of contract
citation: Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136), s 74(1)-(2)
plain: If a contract is broken, the innocent side can claim the losses that would normally flow from that breach, plus losses both sides knew were likely when they signed. Remote and indirect losses are not recoverable at all.
text:
## Text

"74. (1) When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by the breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it.

(2) Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach."

## In plain words

If a contract is broken, the innocent side can claim the losses that would normally flow from that breach, plus losses both sides knew were likely when they signed. Remote and indirect losses are not recoverable at all.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

This is the default position that liability caps and exclusions change. Because remote and indirect loss is already excluded by law, a vendor clause excluding "indirect or consequential loss" mainly confirms the default; the real question is whether the cap or exclusion also cuts out ordinary, direct losses. If you will suffer a specific, unusual loss from a failure, tell the vendor in writing before signing so it is within what "the parties knew".

title: Contracts Act 1950, s 75: compensation where a sum or penalty is named for breach
citation: Contracts Act 1950 (Act 136), s 75
plain: If a contract names a sum payable on breach (liquidated damages, a termination fee, a forfeited deposit), a court awards reasonable compensation up to that sum, not automatically the full sum. The named amount is a ceiling. Since Cubic Electronics, the innocent side need not prove its actual loss; the party in breach must show the sum is unreasonable.
text:
## Text

"75. When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for."

"Explanation—A stipulation for increased interest from the date of default may be a stipulation by way of penalty."

## In plain words

If a contract names a sum payable on breach (liquidated damages, a termination fee, a forfeited deposit), a court awards reasonable compensation up to that sum, not automatically the full sum. The named amount is a ceiling. Since Cubic Electronics, the innocent side need not prove its actual loss; the party in breach must show the sum is unreasonable.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

Look for early-termination fees, "pay all remaining fees for the term" clauses, fixed damages for breach of confidentiality, and penalty interest on late payment. Under Malaysian law these are capped at reasonable compensation, but the burden of proving unreasonableness falls on the party in breach (my-case-cubic-electronics), so a high named sum is still a real risk.

title: Personal Data Protection Act 2010, s 5: the seven principles, and what a data processor must follow
citation: Personal Data Protection Act 2010 (Act 709), s 5(1), (1a), (2), with the Act's definition of 'data processor'
plain: The business that decides why personal data is used (the data controller) must follow all seven principles. A vendor that only handles the data on the controller's behalf (the data processor) must, since the 2024 amendments, itself follow the Security Principle, and breaking it is a criminal offence for either of them.
text:
## Text

"“data processor”, in relation to personal data, means any person, other than an employee of the data controller, who processes the personal data solely on behalf of the data controller, and does not process the personal data for any of his own purposes;"

"5. (1) The processing of personal data by a data controller shall be in compliance with the following Personal Data Protection Principles, namely: (a) the General Principle; (b) the Notice and Choice Principle; (c) the Disclosure Principle; (d) the Security Principle; (e) the Retention Principle; (f) the Data Integrity Principle; and (g) the Access Principle, as set out in sections 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12.

(1a) Where the processing of personal data is carried out by a data processor on behalf of the data controller, the data processor shall comply with the Security Principle as specified in section 9.

(2) Subject to sections 45 and 46, a data controller who contravenes subsection (1) or a data processor who contravenes subsection (1a) commits an offence and shall, on conviction, be liable to a fine not exceeding one million ringgit or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years or to both."

## In plain words

The business that decides why personal data is used (the data controller) must follow all seven principles. A vendor that only handles the data on the controller's behalf (the data processor) must, since the 2024 amendments, itself follow the Security Principle, and breaking it is a criminal offence for either of them.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

When a vendor such as a payroll, CRM or cloud provider will handle your customers' or staff personal data, you remain the controller and stay responsible for all seven principles. The contract should require the vendor to process only on your instructions, meet the security standard in s 9, and help you meet your own duties.

title: Personal Data Protection Act 2010, s 9: the Security Principle for controllers and processors
citation: Personal Data Protection Act 2010 (Act 709), s 9(1)-(2)
plain: Both the business and its data vendor must take practical steps to keep personal data safe, judged by how sensitive the data is, where it is stored, the equipment, the staff who can see it, and how it is transferred. A vendor must give sufficient guarantees about its security measures and take reasonable steps to make sure they are followed.
text:
## Text

"9. (1) A data controller and a data processor shall, when processing personal data, take practical steps to protect the personal data from any loss, misuse, modification, unauthorized or accidental access or disclosure, alteration or destruction by having regard— (a) to the nature of the personal data and the harm that would result from such loss, misuse, modification, unauthorized or accidental access or disclosure, alteration or destruction; (b) to the place or location where the personal data is stored; (c) to any security measures incorporated into any equipment in which the personal data is stored; (d) to the measures taken for ensuring the reliability, integrity and competence of personnel having access to the personal data; and (e) to the measures taken for ensuring the secure transfer of the personal data.

(2) Where processing of personal data is carried out by a data processor on behalf of a data controller, the data processor shall, for the purpose of protecting the personal data from any loss, misuse, modification, unauthorized or accidental access or disclosure, alteration or destruction— (a) provide sufficient guarantees in respect of the technical and organizational security measures governing the processing to be carried out; and (b) take reasonable steps to ensure compliance with those measures."

## In plain words

Both the business and its data vendor must take practical steps to keep personal data safe, judged by how sensitive the data is, where it is stored, the equipment, the staff who can see it, and how it is transferred. A vendor must give sufficient guarantees about its security measures and take reasonable steps to make sure they are followed.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

A data-protection clause that says only "vendor will use industry-standard security" gives you little to point to. Ask for the vendor's security measures to be described or attached, for staff confidentiality, for secure transfer, and for audit or evidence of compliance, which is what s 9(2) expects a processor to guarantee.

title: Personal Data Protection Act 2010, s 12A: appointing a data protection officer
citation: Personal Data Protection Act 2010 (Act 709), s 12A(1)-(2), (4)
plain: Both the business that controls personal data and any vendor processing it for that business must appoint at least one data protection officer. Having a DPO does not remove the company's own legal duties.
text:
## Text

"12A. (1) A data controller shall appoint one or more data protection officers who shall be accountable to the data controller for the compliance with this Act.

(2) Where the processing of personal data is carried out by a data processor on behalf of the data controller, the data processor shall appoint one or more data protection officers who shall be accountable to the data processor for the compliance with this Act.

…

(4) The appointment of data protection officer under subsections (1) and (2) shall not discharge the data controller or data processor from all duties and functions under this Act."

## In plain words

Both the business that controls personal data and any vendor processing it for that business must appoint at least one data protection officer. Having a DPO does not remove the company's own legal duties.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

A data-processing vendor should be able to name its DPO. Asking for the DPO's contact details in the contract, as the point of contact for breaches and data requests, is a simple and reasonable ask.

title: Personal Data Protection Act 2010, s 12B: notifying a personal data breach
citation: Personal Data Protection Act 2010 (Act 709), s 12B(1)-(3)
plain: If a business has reason to believe personal data it controls has been breached, it must tell the Personal Data Protection Commissioner as soon as practicable, and tell affected people if they may suffer significant harm. Failing to notify the Commissioner is an offence. The duty sits on the controller, not the vendor.
text:
## Text

"12B. (1) Where a data controller has reason to believe that a personal data breach has occurred, the data controller shall, as soon as practicable, notify the Commissioner in the manner and form as determined by the Commissioner.

(2) Where the personal data breach under subsection (1) causes or likely to cause any significant harm to the data subject, the data controller shall notify the personal data breach to the data subject in the manner and form as determined by the Commissioner without unnecessary delay.

(3) A data controller who contravenes subsection (1) commits an offence and shall, on conviction, be liable to a fine not exceeding two hundred and fifty thousand ringgit or imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years or to both."

## In plain words

If a business has reason to believe personal data it controls has been breached, it must tell the Personal Data Protection Commissioner as soon as practicable, and tell affected people if they may suffer significant harm. Failing to notify the Commissioner is an offence. The duty sits on the controller, not the vendor.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

Because the legal duty is yours as controller, you can only meet it if your vendor tells you quickly. A service agreement handling personal data should oblige the vendor to notify you promptly (a fixed number of hours is common) and to help with the investigation and the notices.

title: Personal Data Protection Act 2010, s 129: transferring personal data outside Malaysia
citation: Personal Data Protection Act 2010 (Act 709), s 129(2)-(3)
plain: A Malaysian business may send personal data abroad if the destination has a law substantially similar to Malaysia's PDPA or gives at least equivalent protection, or if another listed ground applies, such as the person's consent or necessity for a contract with that person.
text:
## Text

"129. (1) (Deleted by Act A1727).

(2) A data controller may transfer any personal data of a data subject to any place outside Malaysia if— (a) there is in that place in force any law which is substantially similar to this Act; or (b) that place ensures an adequate level of protection in relation to the processing of personal data which is at least equivalent to the level of protection afforded by this Act.

(3) Notwithstanding subsection (2), a data controller may transfer any personal data to a place outside Malaysia if— (a) the data subject has given his consent to the transfer; (b) the transfer is necessary for the performance of a contract between the data subject and the data controller; …"

## In plain words

A Malaysian business may send personal data abroad if the destination has a law substantially similar to Malaysia's PDPA or gives at least equivalent protection, or if another listed ground applies, such as the person's consent or necessity for a contract with that person.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

Cloud and SaaS vendors often store or access data outside Malaysia. The contract should say where data will be stored and accessed, require the vendor to tell you before moving it, and commit it to protection at least equivalent to the PDPA, so you can show s 129 is satisfied.

title: Limitation Act 1953, s 6(1): six years to sue on a contract
citation: Limitation Act 1953 (Act 254), s 6(1)
plain: In Malaysia, a claim for breach of contract must normally be started within six years from when the claim arose, usually the date of the breach. After that, the claim is time-barred.
text:
## Text

"6. (1) Save as hereinafter provided the following actions shall not be brought after the expiration of six years from the date on which the cause of action accrued, that is to say— (a) actions founded on a contract or on tort; (b) actions to enforce a recognisance; (c) actions to enforce an award; (d) actions to recover any sum recoverable by virtue of any written law other than a penalty or forfeiture or of a sum by way of penalty or forfeiture."

## In plain words

In Malaysia, a claim for breach of contract must normally be started within six years from when the claim arose, usually the date of the breach. After that, the claim is time-barred.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

This is the baseline against which to judge a vendor clause such as "any claim must be brought within 12 months". Under Malaysian law a contract term that shortens the time to enforce rights is void to that extent (my-ca1950-s29), so the six-year period normally still applies. Confidentiality breaches are often discovered late, which makes the full period valuable.

title: Evidence Act 1950, s 92: oral statements cannot vary a written contract (with exceptions)
citation: Evidence Act 1950 (Act 56), s 92 and provisos (a), (b), (d)
plain: Once a contract is in writing, what was said in meetings or calls generally cannot be used to contradict or add to it. There are exceptions, for example fraud or mistake, a separate side agreement on something the document does not cover, or a later agreement to change it.
text:
## Text

"92. When the terms of any such contract, grant or other disposition of property, or any matter required by law to be reduced to the form of a document, have been proved according to section 91, no evidence of any oral agreement or statement shall be admitted as between the parties to any such instrument or their representatives in interest for the purpose of contradicting, varying, adding to, or subtracting from its terms:

Provided that— (a) any fact may be proved which would invalidate any document or which would entitle any person to any decree or order relating thereto, such as fraud, intimidation, illegality, want of due execution, want of capacity in any contracting party, the fact that it is wrongly dated, want or failure of consideration, or mistake in fact or law;

(b) the existence of any separate oral agreement, as to any matter on which a document is silent and which is not inconsistent with its terms, may be proved, and in considering whether or not this proviso applies, the court shall have regard to the degree of formality of the document;

…

(d) the existence of any distinct subsequent oral agreement, to rescind or modify any such contract, grant or disposition of property, may be proved except in cases in which the contract, grant or disposition of property is by law required to be in writing, or has been registered according to the law in force …"

## In plain words

Once a contract is in writing, what was said in meetings or calls generally cannot be used to contradict or add to it. There are exceptions, for example fraud or mistake, a separate side agreement on something the document does not cover, or a later agreement to change it.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

Promises a salesperson made ("we'll include support", "you can cancel any time") may not count unless they are in the signed document, and an entire-agreement clause makes that even clearer. If a promise matters, get it written into the contract or an order form.

title: Cubic Electronics Sdn Bhd (in liquidation) v Mars Telecommunications Sdn Bhd: liquidated damages under s 75
citation: [2019] 6 MLJ 15; [2018] MLJU 1935 (Federal Court of Malaysia, decided 21 November 2018)
plain: In Malaysia, a fixed sum for breach (liquidated damages, a forfeited deposit, a termination fee) can now be claimed without proving the actual loss. The side that broke the contract has to prove the sum is unreasonable. The court can still cut it down to reasonable compensation, and the named sum is the maximum.
text:
## Text

Summary: Mars paid RM 3.04 million of earnest deposits and interest towards buying land from Cubic, failed to sign the sale agreement after four extensions, and Cubic forfeited the sum. The Federal Court overturned the long-standing view in Selva Kumar (1995) that actual loss must always be proved, and held that s 75 applies to forfeiture of deposits as well as damages clauses.

Holding, as summarised in the source note: "The Federal Court decided that Section 75 allowed compensation as agreed by the parties in the liquidated damages clause, irrespective of whether actual loss or damage is proven, provided that the provision made is not extravagant, exorbitant or unconscionable and such liquidated damages claims are then enforceable. The innocent party needs only to show that there was a breach of contract. The onus then lies on the defaulting party to prove that the sum stipulated in the liquidated damages clause is unreasonable."

Para 70 of the judgment, as quoted in the practitioner blog named in licence_note: "The initial onus lies on the party seeking to enforce a clause under section 75 of the Act to adduce evidence that firstly, there was a breach of contract and that secondly, the contract contains a clause specifying a sum to be paid upon breach. Once these two elements have been established, the innocent party is entitled to receive a sum not exceeding the amount stipulated in the contract irrespective of whether actual damage or loss is proven, subject always to the defaulting party proving the unreasonableness of the damages clause including the sum stated therein, if any."

## In plain words

In Malaysia, a fixed sum for breach (liquidated damages, a forfeited deposit, a termination fee) can now be claimed without proving the actual loss. The side that broke the contract has to prove the sum is unreasonable. The court can still cut it down to reasonable compensation, and the named sum is the maximum.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

A high early-termination fee or fixed damages for breach of confidentiality is more dangerous after Cubic Electronics, because the burden of showing it is unreasonable sits on the party in breach. Negotiate the number before signing rather than counting on a court to reduce it. Applies with s 75 (my-ca1950-s75).

title: CIMB Bank Bhd v Anthony Lawrence Bourke & Anor: an exclusion clause that leaves no remedy is void under s 29
citation: [2019] 2 MLJ 1 (Federal Court of Malaysia)
plain: Under Malaysian law, a clause that would leave the innocent party with no remedy at all for a proven breach can be struck down as void under s 29. The question is whether, on the facts, the clause absolutely blocks the claim. The case does not say that every cap or exclusion is invalid.
text:
## Text

Summary: the bank failed to make a progress payment under a housing loan, the purchase fell through, and the borrowers sued. The bank relied on a clause excluding loss of income, profit, savings and indirect or consequential damages. The High Court upheld the clause; the Court of Appeal and then the Federal Court did not.

Holding, as summarised in the source note: "in a unanimous 5 panel decision, the Federal Court upheld the Court of Appeal’s decision and affirmed that where an exclusion clause in an agreement sought to (1) exonerate a contract breaker of its liability for a breach of that contract and (2) negates the contract breakers’ liability to pay compensation for non-performance of that contract, it would be void. Section 29 of the Contracts Act, 1950 may be invoked to strike down and invalidate such a clause."

## In plain words

Under Malaysian law, a clause that would leave the innocent party with no remedy at all for a proven breach can be struck down as void under s 29. The question is whether, on the facts, the clause absolutely blocks the claim. The case does not say that every cap or exclusion is invalid.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

Vendor terms that exclude "all liability" or every realistic head of loss for the vendor's own breach are open to challenge in Malaysia. A mutual cap that still leaves a meaningful remedy is a different question that this case did not decide. Use the case to argue for a real, mutual cap rather than a total exclusion.

title: Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977, s 1(3) and First Schedule para 1(c): business liability only, and IP terms excluded
citation: Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 (2020 Rev Ed), s 1(3); First Schedule, para 1(c)
plain: Singapore's Unfair Contract Terms Act controls exclusion clauses only for liability arising in the course of a business, which covers ordinary B2B vendor contracts. But its main controls (ss 2 to 4) do not apply to the parts of a contract that create, transfer or end rights in intellectual property, including "technical or commercial information".
text:
## Text

"1.— … (3) In the case of both contract and tort, sections 2 to 7 apply (except where the contrary is stated in section 6(4)) only to business liability, that is liability for breach of obligations or duties arising from things done or to be done by a person in the course of a business (whether his own business or another’s), and references to liability are to be read accordingly."

First Schedule: "1. Sections 2 to 4 do not extend to — … (c) any contract so far as it relates to the creation or transfer of a right or interest in any patent, trade mark, copyright, registered design, technical or commercial information or other intellectual property, or relates to the termination of any such right or interest;"

## In plain words

Singapore's Unfair Contract Terms Act controls exclusion clauses only for liability arising in the course of a business, which covers ordinary B2B vendor contracts. But its main controls (ss 2 to 4) do not apply to the parts of a contract that create, transfer or end rights in intellectual property, including "technical or commercial information".

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

An NDA is largely about "technical or commercial information", and IP assignment or licence clauses in service agreements are about IP rights. For those parts, an exclusion clause may fall outside UCTA's reasonableness controls, so the wording you agree is more likely to stand. The service-delivery parts of the contract remain covered.

title: Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977, s 2: excluding liability for negligence
citation: Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 (2020 Rev Ed), s 2
plain: In Singapore, a business can never contract out of liability for death or personal injury caused by its negligence. For other losses caused by negligence (including careless performance of a contract), an exclusion or cap only works if it passes the reasonableness test in s 11.
text:
## Text

"2.—(1) A person cannot by reference to any contract term or to a notice given to persons generally or to particular persons exclude or restrict his liability for death or personal injury resulting from negligence.

(2) In the case of other loss or damage, a person cannot so exclude or restrict his liability for negligence except in so far as the term or notice satisfies the requirement of reasonableness.

(3) Where a contract term or notice purports to exclude or restrict liability for negligence, a person’s agreement to or awareness of it is not of itself to be taken as indicating his voluntary acceptance of any risk."

## In plain words

In Singapore, a business can never contract out of liability for death or personal injury caused by its negligence. For other losses caused by negligence (including careless performance of a contract), an exclusion or cap only works if it passes the reasonableness test in s 11.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

A vendor clause excluding "all liability howsoever arising, including negligence" is subject to the reasonableness test, and the vendor has to prove it is reasonable (sg-ucta1977-s11). The usual carve-out "nothing limits liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence" reflects s 2(1); its absence is a drafting red flag.

title: Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977, s 3: exclusions in the other side's written standard terms
citation: Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 (2020 Rev Ed), s 3
plain: When a business signs up on a vendor's own written standard terms, the vendor can only rely on a clause that limits its liability for its own breach, or lets it deliver something substantially different or nothing at all, if that clause is reasonable.
text:
## Text

"3.—(1) This section applies as between contracting parties where one of them deals as consumer or on the other’s written standard terms of business.

(2) As against that party, the other cannot by reference to any contract term —
(a) when himself in breach of contract, exclude or restrict any liability of his in respect of the breach; or
(b) claim to be entitled —
(i) to render a contractual performance substantially different from that which was reasonably expected of him; or
(ii) in respect of the whole or any part of his contractual obligation, to render no performance at all,
except in so far as (in any of the cases mentioned in this subsection) the contract term satisfies the requirement of reasonableness."

## In plain words

When a business signs up on a vendor's own written standard terms, the vendor can only rely on a clause that limits its liability for its own breach, or lets it deliver something substantially different or nothing at all, if that clause is reasonable.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

This is the section that protects an SME signing a vendor's click-through or standard service terms. Clauses such as "vendor may change or discontinue the service at any time" or "vendor's liability for breach is limited to one month's fees" must pass the reasonableness test. A heavily negotiated, bespoke contract may fall outside s 3.

title: Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977, s 11: the reasonableness test, caps and burden of proof
citation: Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 (2020 Rev Ed), s 11(1), (4), (5)
plain: A limiting term is reasonable only if it was fair to include it, judged by what both sides knew or should have known when they signed. For a cap at a fixed sum, the court looks especially at the resources the party relying on it could expect to have and whether it could have insured. The party relying on the clause must prove it is reasonable.
text:
## Text

"11.—(1) In relation to a contract term, the requirement of reasonableness for the purposes of this Part and section 3 of the Misrepresentation Act 1967 is that the term shall have been a fair and reasonable one to be included having regard to the circumstances which were, or ought reasonably to have been, known to or in the contemplation of the parties when the contract was made.

…

(4) Where by reference to a contract term or notice a person seeks to restrict liability to a specified sum of money, and the question arises (under this or any other Act) whether the term or notice satisfies the requirement of reasonableness, regard shall be had in particular (but without prejudice to subsection (2) in the case of contract terms) to —
(a) the resources which he could expect to be available to him for the purpose of meeting the liability should it arise; and
(b) how far it was open to him to cover himself by insurance.

(5) It is for those claiming that a contract term or notice satisfies the requirement of reasonableness to show that it does."

## In plain words

A limiting term is reasonable only if it was fair to include it, judged by what both sides knew or should have known when they signed. For a cap at a fixed sum, the court looks especially at the resources the party relying on it could expect to have and whether it could have insured. The party relying on the clause must prove it is reasonable.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

Use this when a vendor's cap is tiny compared with the harm its failure could cause. A well-resourced or insured vendor will find it harder to justify a very low cap, and it carries the burden of proof. Keep a record of what you told the vendor about your risks during negotiation.

title: Misrepresentation Act 1967, s 3: excluding liability for pre-contract misrepresentation
citation: Misrepresentation Act 1967 (2020 Rev Ed), s 3
plain: If a contract tries to exclude liability for false statements made before signing, that term only works if it is reasonable, and the party relying on it must prove that. This applies to all contracts, not only standard terms.
text:
## Text

"3. If a contract contains a term which would exclude or restrict —
(a) any liability to which a party to a contract may be subject by reason of any misrepresentation made by him before the contract was made; or
(b) any remedy available to another party to the contract by reason of such a misrepresentation,
that term shall be of no effect except in so far as it satisfies the requirement of reasonableness as stated in section 11(1) of the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977, and it is for those claiming that the term satisfies that requirement to show that it does."

## In plain words

If a contract tries to exclude liability for false statements made before signing, that term only works if it is reasonable, and the party relying on it must prove that. This applies to all contracts, not only standard terms.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

Vendor terms often say "the customer has not relied on any statement not set out in this agreement" alongside an entire-agreement clause. In Singapore, a term that excludes liability for misrepresentation has to pass s 3; an entire-agreement clause on its own may not be enough (see sg-case-lee-chee-wei). If a sales claim matters to you, write it into the contract.

title: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, s 2(1) and s 4(2)-(3): data intermediaries and who stays responsible
citation: Personal Data Protection Act 2012 (2020 Rev Ed), s 2(1) ('data intermediary'), s 4(2)-(3)
plain: A vendor that processes personal data for your business under a written contract is a "data intermediary". It has only a few direct duties: protect the data (s 24), do not keep it longer than needed (s 25), and report breaches to you (s 26C(3)(a)). Your business keeps every other PDPA obligation as if it did the processing itself.
text:
## Text

"“data intermediary” means an organisation which processes personal data on behalf of another organisation but does not include an employee of that other organisation;"

"4.— … (2) Parts 3, 4, 5, 6 (except sections 24 and 25), 6A (except sections 26C(3)(a) and 26E) and 6B do not impose any obligation on a data intermediary in respect of its processing of personal data on behalf of and for the purposes of another organisation pursuant to a contract which is evidenced or made in writing.

(3) An organisation has the same obligation under this Act in respect of personal data processed on its behalf and for its purposes by a data intermediary as if the personal data were processed by the organisation itself."

## In plain words

A vendor that processes personal data for your business under a written contract is a "data intermediary". It has only a few direct duties: protect the data (s 24), do not keep it longer than needed (s 25), and report breaches to you (s 26C(3)(a)). Your business keeps every other PDPA obligation as if it did the processing itself.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

Because you remain responsible for what your vendor does with personal data, the service agreement is where you push your other duties onto it: process only on your instructions, limit use and disclosure, help with access and correction requests, and control overseas transfers. The written contract is also what puts the vendor in the lighter data-intermediary regime.

title: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, s 24: the protection obligation
citation: Personal Data Protection Act 2012 (2020 Rev Ed), s 24
plain: Any organisation holding or controlling personal data must make reasonable security arrangements to stop it being accessed, used, copied or changed without authority, and to stop devices holding it being lost. This duty applies directly to vendors acting as data intermediaries too.
text:
## Text

"24. An organisation must protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent —
(a) unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal, or similar risks; and
(b) the loss of any storage medium or device on which personal data is stored."

## In plain words

Any organisation holding or controlling personal data must make reasonable security arrangements to stop it being accessed, used, copied or changed without authority, and to stop devices holding it being lost. This duty applies directly to vendors acting as data intermediaries too.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

A data-protection or security clause should set out what "reasonable security arrangements" means for the service, for example encryption, access control and incident handling, because both you and the vendor are bound by s 24 and you are also responsible for the vendor's processing (sg-pdpa2012-data-intermediary).

title: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, s 25: the retention limitation obligation
citation: Personal Data Protection Act 2012 (2020 Rev Ed), s 25
plain: Personal data must be deleted or anonymised once it no longer serves the purpose it was collected for and is not needed for legal or business reasons. Like s 24, this applies directly to data intermediaries.
text:
## Text

"25. An organisation must cease to retain its documents containing personal data, or remove the means by which the personal data can be associated with particular individuals, as soon as it is reasonable to assume that —
(a) the purpose for which that personal data was collected is no longer being served by retention of the personal data; and
(b) retention is no longer necessary for legal or business purposes."

## In plain words

Personal data must be deleted or anonymised once it no longer serves the purpose it was collected for and is not needed for legal or business reasons. Like s 24, this applies directly to data intermediaries.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

The end-of-contract clause should require the vendor to return or delete your personal data, and certify deletion, within a set time after termination. A vendor clause allowing it to keep your data indefinitely "for its business purposes" conflicts with this duty.

title: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, s 26C(3): a data intermediary must report a breach without undue delay
citation: Personal Data Protection Act 2012 (2020 Rev Ed), s 26C(2)-(3)
plain: When a vendor processing your personal data suspects a breach, the law requires it to tell you without undue delay. Your business must then assess, reasonably and quickly, whether the breach is serious enough to be notifiable.
text:
## Text

"26C.— … (2) Subject to subsection (3), where an organisation has reason to believe that a data breach affecting personal data in its possession or under its control has occurred, the organisation must conduct, in a reasonable and expeditious manner, an assessment of whether the data breach is a notifiable data breach.

(3) Where a data intermediary (other than a data intermediary mentioned in section 26E) has reason to believe that a data breach has occurred in relation to personal data that the data intermediary is processing on behalf of and for the purposes of another organisation —
(a) the data intermediary must, without undue delay, notify that other organisation of the occurrence of the data breach; and
(b) that other organisation must, upon notification by the data intermediary, conduct an assessment of whether the data breach is a notifiable data breach."

## In plain words

When a vendor processing your personal data suspects a breach, the law requires it to tell you without undue delay. Your business must then assess, reasonably and quickly, whether the breach is serious enough to be notifiable.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

"Without undue delay" is the legal floor. Because your own clock to notify the PDPC starts after your assessment (sg-pdpa2012-s26d), ask for a specific vendor notice period (for example 24 to 48 hours), the details the vendor must provide, and its cooperation with your assessment.

title: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, s 26D(1)-(2): notify the Commission within 3 calendar days
citation: Personal Data Protection Act 2012 (2020 Rev Ed), s 26D(1)-(2)
plain: Once your business decides a breach is notifiable, it must tell the Personal Data Protection Commission as soon as practicable and within 3 calendar days at the latest, and usually tell the affected individuals too.
text:
## Text

"26D.—(1) Where an organisation assesses, in accordance with section 26C, that a data breach is a notifiable data breach, the organisation must notify the Commission as soon as is practicable, but in any case no later than 3 calendar days after the day the organisation makes that assessment.

(2) Subject to subsections (5), (6) and (7), on or after notifying the Commission under subsection (1), the organisation must also notify each affected individual affected by a notifiable data breach mentioned in section 26B(1)(a) in any manner that is reasonable in the circumstances."

## In plain words

Once your business decides a breach is notifiable, it must tell the Personal Data Protection Commission as soon as practicable and within 3 calendar days at the latest, and usually tell the affected individuals too.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

You cannot meet a 3-day deadline if your vendor is slow to tell you or to share facts. Tie the vendor's notice and cooperation duties in the contract to this timeline, and consider who pays for notification costs when the breach is the vendor's fault.

title: Limitation Act 1959, s 6(1): six years to sue on a contract
citation: Limitation Act 1959 (2020 Rev Ed), s 6(1)
plain: In Singapore, a claim for breach of contract must normally be started within 6 years from when the claim arose, usually the date of the breach.

title: Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 2001, s 2: when a non-party can enforce a contract term
citation: Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 2001 (2020 Rev Ed), s 2(1)-(4)
plain: Under Singapore law, someone who did not sign the contract can enforce a term if the contract says they may, or if the term is meant to benefit them and they are identified by name, class or description, unless the contract shows the parties did not intend that.
text:
## Text

"2.—(1) Subject to the provisions of this Act, a person who is not a party to a contract (called in this Act a third party) may, in the third party’s own right, enforce a term of the contract if —
(a) the contract expressly provides that the third party may; or
(b) subject to subsection (2), the term purports to confer a benefit on the third party.

(2) Subsection (1)(b) does not apply if, on a proper construction of the contract, it appears that the parties did not intend the term to be enforceable by the third party.

(3) The third party must be expressly identified in the contract by name, as a member of a class or as answering a particular description, but need not be in existence when the contract is entered into.

(4) This section does not confer a right on a third party to enforce a term of a contract otherwise than subject to and in accordance with any other relevant terms of the contract."

## In plain words

Under Singapore law, someone who did not sign the contract can enforce a term if the contract says they may, or if the term is meant to benefit them and they are identified by name, class or description, unless the contract shows the parties did not intend that.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

Clauses protecting a party's "affiliates", "group companies" or "customers" (for example an indemnity or confidentiality duty owed to them) may be enforceable by those entities directly. Most standard contracts include a clause excluding third-party rights; check whether you want it, especially if your group companies need to rely on the NDA.

title: Denka Advantech Pte Ltd v Seraya Energy Pte Ltd: Singapore keeps the Dunlop penalty test
citation: [2020] SGCA 119 (Court of Appeal, Civil Appeals Nos 37, 38, 100 and 101 of 2019; judgment 15 December 2020)
plain: In Singapore, a fixed sum payable on breach is enforceable if, when the contract was made, it was a genuine pre-estimate of the likely loss; if not, it is an unenforceable penalty. The rule applies only to sums triggered by a breach, so a fee payable on some other event (such as exercising an option to terminate) is not tested this way.
text:
## Text

Summary: Seraya claimed liquidated damages (LD) under electricity retailer agreements (ERAs) with Denka, in a dispute that also turned on whether Denka had breached them. The Court of Appeal declined to follow the UK Supreme Court's restatement in Cavendish v Makdessi and the Australian approach in Andrews.

At [185]: "(a) First, the Penalty Rule applies only in the context of a breach of contract. This does not preclude the applicability of other doctrines (including the narrow doctrine of unconscionability in BOM v BOK ([98] supra)) from operating where relevant.
(b) Secondly, the legal criteria to ascertain whether the Penalty Rule applies may be found in the statement of principles enunciated by Lord Dunedin in Dunlop ([1] supra). The focus is whether the clause concerned provided a genuine pre-estimate of the likely loss at the time of contracting. In this regard, the only “legitimate interest” which the Penalty Rule is concerned with is that of compensation."

At [309]: "In sum, we are satisfied that the LD clauses are not penalties."

## In plain words

In Singapore, a fixed sum payable on breach is enforceable if, when the contract was made, it was a genuine pre-estimate of the likely loss; if not, it is an unenforceable penalty. The rule applies only to sums triggered by a breach, so a fee payable on some other event (such as exercising an option to terminate) is not tested this way.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

Ask how a vendor's liquidated damages or early-termination sum was worked out. Under Singapore law a sum triggered by your breach that bears no relation to likely loss can be challenged, but a fee drafted as the price of an option rather than as a sum for breach may escape the rule. Contrast Malaysia, where s 75 and Cubic Electronics apply instead (my-case-cubic-electronics).

title: Man Financial (S) Pte Ltd v Wong Bark Chuan David: restraint of trade needs a legitimate interest and must go no further than necessary
citation: [2007] SGCA 53 (Court of Appeal, CA 17/2007; decision 29 November 2007)
plain: In Singapore a non-compete or non-solicit is not automatically void, as it is in Malaysia, but it is enforceable only if it protects a real business interest (such as goodwill, trade secrets, trade connections) and goes no further than needed in scope, area and time. A bare ban on competing protects nothing and fails.
text:
## Text

Summary: a former CEO's termination agreement contained non-solicitation and non-competition clauses. The Court of Appeal restated the Singapore doctrine of restraint of trade, applying Lord Macnaghten's reasonableness test in Nordenfelt, and agreed with the trial judge that there was insufficient evidence of a legitimate proprietary interest behind the non-competition clause (Clause C.3), which was also far too wide in area.

At [79]: "There must always – and this is a fundamental legal proposition in this particular area of the law – be a legitimate proprietary interest which the court will then seek to protect by way of the doctrine of restraint of trade … However, even where a legitimate proprietary interest is shown, the court will ensure that the covenant in restraint of trade goes no further than what is necessary to protect the interest concerned."

At [80]: "In the context of the sale of a business, the main legitimate proprietary interest is that of goodwill."

## In plain words

In Singapore a non-compete or non-solicit is not automatically void, as it is in Malaysia, but it is enforceable only if it protects a real business interest (such as goodwill, trade secrets, trade connections) and goes no further than needed in scope, area and time. A bare ban on competing protects nothing and fails.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

A non-compete inside an NDA usually adds nothing a confidentiality clause does not already protect, which makes it hard to justify under this test; the judgment also says that where confidential information is already covered by another clause, the restraint must protect something more. Ask for it to be removed, or narrowed to a specific product, area and short period.

title: Sembcorp Marine Ltd v PPL Holdings Pte Ltd: the three-step test for implying terms
citation: [2013] SGCA 43 (Court of Appeal, Civil Appeals Nos 75 and 77 of 2012; decision 25 July 2013)
plain: A Singapore court will add a term the contract does not state only if the parties never thought about the gap, the contract does not work commercially without it, and both sides would obviously have said "of course" to it. A term is not implied just because it would be fair or sensible.
text:
## Text

Summary: in a joint-venture dispute, Sembcorp argued for an implied term (the "Equality Premise Clause") about the consequences of a shareholder ceasing to hold at least 50% of the joint-venture company. The Court of Appeal set out the approach to implied terms, stressing that the test is necessity, not reasonableness.

At [101]: "It follows from these points that the implication of terms is to be considered using a three-step process:
(a) The first step is to ascertain how the gap in the contract arises. Implication will be considered only if the court discerns that the gap arose because the parties did not contemplate the gap.
(b) At the second step, the court considers whether it is necessary in the business or commercial sense to imply a term in order to give the contract efficacy.
(c) Finally, the court considers the specific term to be implied. This must be one which the parties, having regard to the need for business efficacy, would have responded “Oh, of course!” had the proposed term been put to them at time of the contract. If it is not possible to find such a clear response, then, the gap persists and the consequences of that gap ensue."

## In plain words

A Singapore court will add a term the contract does not state only if the parties never thought about the gap, the contract does not work commercially without it, and both sides would obviously have said "of course" to it. A term is not implied just because it would be fair or sensible.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

Do not rely on a court to fill gaps such as missing service levels, exit assistance, data return or a right to terminate for convenience. If something matters, it needs to be written into the contract, because a missing term is unlikely to be implied.

title: Lee Chee Wei v Tan Hor Peow Victor: the effect of an entire-agreement clause
citation: [2007] SGCA 22 (Court of Appeal, CA 88/2006 and 91/2006; decision 16 April 2007)
plain: An entire-agreement clause generally means the signed document is the whole deal, so promises made during negotiations cannot be used to add to it. How far a particular clause goes depends on its exact words.
text:
## Text

Summary: in a dispute over a share sale agreement, one party argued for an unwritten condition based on negotiations. The Court of Appeal rejected it, and then set out the principles on entire-agreement clauses, the agreement containing one ("This Agreement sets forth the entire agreement and understanding between the Parties in connection with the matters dealt with and described herein").

At [25]: "Entire agreement clauses appear as a smorgasbord of variously worded provisions. The effect of each clause is essentially a matter of contractual interpretation and will necessarily depend upon its precise wording and context. Generally, such clauses are conducive to certainty as they define and confine the parties’ rights and obligations within the four corners of the written document thereby precluding any attempt to qualify or supplement the document by reference to pre-contractual representations."

## In plain words

An entire-agreement clause generally means the signed document is the whole deal, so promises made during negotiations cannot be used to add to it. How far a particular clause goes depends on its exact words.

## When it matters in an NDA or service agreement

Almost every vendor contract has an entire-agreement clause. Anything the salesperson promised, such as features, support hours, or a free exit, should be written into the contract or an attached schedule, or you may not be able to rely on it. Excluding liability for misrepresentation is a separate step that must also pass Misrepresentation Act s 3 (sg-ma1967-s3).

title: Confidentiality: what counts as secret, and the exceptions (NDA)
plain: This is the heart of an NDA. It says what information is protected, what the receiving side may do with it, who else may see it, and which information is never treated as secret.
text:
clause_type: `confidentiality` · contract_type: `nda`

## In plain words
This is the heart of an NDA. It says what information is protected, what the receiving side may do
with it, who else may see it, and which information is never treated as secret.

## What balanced looks like
- **Mutual** when both sides will share information. A one-way NDA is fine only when one side
  genuinely shares nothing.
- **A clear definition.** Information counts as confidential if it is marked confidential, or if a
  sensible person would understand it to be confidential from its nature.
- **Use limited to the purpose.** The receiver may use the information only to evaluate or carry out
  the stated deal.
- **Need-to-know sharing.** The receiver may share with its staff, advisers and contractors who need
  it for the purpose and who are bound by similar confidentiality duties.
- **Reasonable care.** Protect it at least as carefully as your own similar information.
- **The standard exceptions ("carve-outs").** The duty does not cover information that:
  1. is or becomes public without the receiver's fault;
  2. the receiver already knew before it was disclosed;
  3. the receiver gets lawfully from someone else who owed no duty of secrecy;
  4. the receiver develops independently, without using the disclosed information.
- **Compelled disclosure.** The receiver may disclose if a law, regulator or court requires it,
  after telling the discloser first where allowed, so the discloser can object.

## Red flags
- **High:** no carve-outs at all, or wording that the duty applies "without exception".
- **High:** a definition covering "all information of any kind", including information the receiver
  already had or that is public.
- **High:** no right to disclose when the law requires it, which can put the receiver in breach of
  either the contract or the law.
- **Medium:** one-way obligations when both sides will in fact share information.
- **Medium:** the receiver may not share even with its own lawyers, accountants or staff.
- **Low:** oral disclosures must be confirmed in writing within a short window (common, but note it).

## Suggested ask
"Please make the obligations mutual, limit confidential information to what is marked or obviously
confidential, and add the four standard exceptions plus a right to disclose where the law requires."

title: Term: how long the NDA and the secrecy duty last (NDA)
plain: Two different clocks. The **agreement term** is the window during which information may be shared under the NDA. The **confidentiality period** is how long the receiver must keep it secret after that.
text:
clause_type: `term` · contract_type: `nda`

## In plain words
Two different clocks. The **agreement term** is the window during which information may be shared
under the NDA. The **confidentiality period** is how long the receiver must keep it secret after
that.

## What balanced looks like
- Agreement term of **1 to 2 years**, or until the deal is signed or abandoned.
- Confidentiality period of **2 to 3 years** after disclosure or after the NDA ends. Two years is the
  most common fixed period in published market surveys.
- **Up to 5 years** can be reasonable for very sensitive material, but it should be a deliberate
  choice, not a default.
- **Trade secrets** (for example source code or a secret recipe) may stay protected for as long as
  they remain secret. That is a narrow, reasonable exception.
- The same periods apply to both sides.

## Red flags
- **High:** confidentiality that lasts "in perpetuity", "indefinitely" or "forever" for **all**
  information, not only trade secrets. The receiver then carries the risk of breach for ever.
- **Medium:** a 5-year or longer period for ordinary business information, especially when only one
  side is bound.
- **Medium:** the clock starts only when the discloser says so, or restarts every time new
  information is shared.
- **Low:** no stated term at all; ask for one so everyone knows when duties end.

## Suggested ask
"Please set the confidentiality period to two (or at most three) years after disclosure, with
longer protection only for genuine trade secrets."

title: Termination, and return or destruction of information (NDA)
plain: How either side can end the NDA, and what happens to the shared information when it ends.
text:
clause_type: `termination` · contract_type: `nda`

## In plain words
How either side can end the NDA, and what happens to the shared information when it ends.

## What balanced looks like
- **Either side may end** the NDA by written notice at any time. Ending it stops new disclosures; the
  secrecy duty for information already shared continues for the agreed period.
- **On request or on termination**, the receiver returns or destroys the information and, if asked,
  confirms this in writing.
- **Practical exception:** copies kept in automatic backups, or kept because a law requires it, need
  not be hunted down, but they stay confidential.
- No fee or penalty for walking away from the discussions.

## Red flags
- **High:** only the discloser may end the NDA, while the receiver stays bound with no end date.
- **Medium:** the receiver must certify destruction of every copy, including backups, within a very
  short time (for example 48 hours).
- **Medium:** walking away from the deal triggers a payment or a "break fee".
- **Low:** no written confirmation process; usually harmless.

## Suggested ask
"Please let either party end the NDA by written notice, and allow copies held in routine backups or
kept by law to be retained, provided they stay confidential."

title: Non-compete inside an NDA
plain: A non-compete stops a business from working in a market, or with competitors, for a period. It is a much bigger promise than keeping information secret.
text:
clause_type: `non_compete` · contract_type: `nda`

## In plain words
A non-compete stops a business from working in a market, or with competitors, for a period. It is a
much bigger promise than keeping information secret.

## What balanced looks like
- **A standard NDA has no non-compete at all.** It protects information, not market position.
- Many standard forms say the opposite: the receiver remains free to build or buy similar products,
  as long as it does not misuse the confidential information.
- Where a business restriction is genuinely needed (for example in an exclusive distribution deal),
  it belongs in the main commercial agreement, negotiated openly, short, and limited to a specific
  product and territory.

## Background (general, not advice)
- In **Malaysia**, section 28 of the Contracts Act 1950 says an agreement that restrains someone from
  carrying on a lawful business is void, with narrow exceptions such as the sale of a business's
  goodwill.
- In **Singapore**, a restraint is enforceable only if it protects a legitimate interest and is
  reasonable in scope, area and time.
- Even a restraint that may not hold up in court can deter a small business, cost money to fight, or
  be enforceable under a foreign governing law.

## Red flags
- **High:** any clause that stops the receiver from doing business in a sector, region or with named
  companies, especially under a vague heading such as "Protection of Business Interests".
- **High:** a restriction lasting years after the NDA, or across a whole region (for example "Southeast
  Asia").
- **Medium:** a promise not to deal with the discloser's customers or suppliers.

## Suggested ask
"Please delete the non-compete wording; this NDA should only protect confidential information, and
either party should stay free to do business as long as it does not misuse that information."

title: Non-solicitation of staff (NDA)
plain: A promise not to approach the other side's employees to hire them away. It is common in NDAs and usually acceptable when it is narrow.
text:
clause_type: `non_solicit` · contract_type: `nda`

## In plain words
A promise not to approach the other side's employees to hire them away. It is common in NDAs and
usually acceptable when it is narrow.

## What balanced looks like
- **Mutual**: both sides make the same promise.
- **Short**: 6 to 12 months after the NDA ends.
- **Narrow**: covers only employees the other side actually met or worked with during the
  discussions.
- **Carve-out for general hiring**: job adverts and recruiters not aimed at the other side's staff do
  not count, and neither does hiring someone who applies on their own initiative.

## Red flags
- **Medium:** one-way, protecting only the discloser.
- **Medium:** lasting 24 months or longer, or covering all employees of all group companies.
- **Medium:** extending to customers, suppliers or "business partners" (this starts to look like a
  non-compete; see `non_compete.md`).
- **Low:** no carve-out for general job adverts.

## Suggested ask
"Please make the non-solicitation mutual, limit it to 12 months and to staff involved in our
discussions, and exclude general job adverts and unsolicited applications."

title: Liability and remedies, including fixed damages (NDA)
plain: What happens if someone breaks the NDA: what they must pay, and what the other side can ask a court to do.
text:
clause_type: `liability` · contract_type: `nda`

## In plain words
What happens if someone breaks the NDA: what they must pay, and what the other side can ask a court
to do.

## What balanced looks like
- **Ordinary remedies**: the injured side can claim the loss it can actually prove.
- **Injunction**: both sides accept that a court may order a stop to a breach quickly, because money
  may not fix leaked secrets. This is standard and fair.
- **No fixed damages sum.** Most standard NDAs do not set a pre-agreed amount payable per breach.
- **The same rules for both sides.**
- Often no cap on liability for misuse of confidential information. That is normal in an NDA because
  each side controls its own risk by not leaking.

## Background (general, not advice)
- A fixed sum payable on breach is called **liquidated damages**. In **Malaysia**, section 75 of the
  Contracts Act 1950 lets a court award reasonable compensation up to the stated sum, not
  automatically the whole sum. In **Singapore**, a sum that is a punishment rather than a genuine
  pre-estimate of loss is generally unenforceable (the penalty rule).
- Even so, a large stated sum shifts negotiating power and may be enforceable under a foreign law.

## Red flags
- **High:** a fixed sum payable "for each breach" with no overall limit, or a sum far above any
  realistic loss.
- **High:** the receiver must pay the discloser's legal costs on an indemnity basis, plus damages,
  for any alleged breach, without the discloser having to prove loss.
- **Medium:** only one side is liable; the other side's breaches have no consequence.
- **Medium:** the receiver indemnifies the discloser for "all losses" connected with the NDA.

## Suggested ask
"Please remove the liquidated damages clause and rely on ordinary damages and injunctions, which
apply equally to both parties."

title: Ownership of ideas and no licence (NDA)
plain: Who owns the information and any ideas that come up during the discussions. ("IP" means intellectual property: inventions, designs, software, brands and know-how.)
text:
clause_type: `ip_ownership` · contract_type: `nda`

## In plain words
Who owns the information and any ideas that come up during the discussions. ("IP" means intellectual
property: inventions, designs, software, brands and know-how.)

## What balanced looks like
- Each side **keeps ownership** of what it discloses. Sharing it gives no licence (permission) to use
  it beyond the purpose.
- Each side **keeps the right to develop its own products**, including similar ones, provided it does
  not misuse the other's information.
- No transfer of ownership in anything either side creates on its own.
- Feedback or suggestions given in passing are either left out, or may be used freely by the side
  that receives them, without passing ownership of the giver's own IP.

## Red flags
- **High:** anything the receiver creates, improves or "derives" during the discussions becomes the
  discloser's property.
- **High:** a "residuals" clause that lets the receiver freely use whatever its staff remember. This
  quietly undoes the NDA for the discloser.
- **Medium:** the receiver must assign ownership of feedback, suggestions or improvements to the
  discloser.
- **Low:** silence on ownership; the default (each keeps its own) usually applies.

## Suggested ask
"Please confirm that each party keeps ownership of its own information and anything it develops
independently, and remove any transfer of ownership of improvements or feedback."

title: Governing law: which country's law applies (NDA)
plain: The governing law decides which country's rules are used to read the contract. The jurisdiction wording decides where a court case would be heard. Together they decide how expensive and unfamiliar any dispute would be.
text:
clause_type: `governing_law` · contract_type: `nda`

## In plain words
The governing law decides which country's rules are used to read the contract. The jurisdiction
wording decides where a court case would be heard. Together they decide how expensive and
unfamiliar any dispute would be.

## What balanced looks like
- For two Malaysian companies: **Malaysian law**, courts in Malaysia (often Kuala Lumpur).
- For a Malaysian and a Singaporean company: **Malaysian or Singapore law**, with the matching
  courts. Both are common, familiar and close to home.
- Either side may still seek an urgent injunction in any court where the other side is.
- Non-exclusive jurisdiction is friendlier than exclusive jurisdiction in a far-away court.

## Red flags
- **High:** the law and **exclusive** courts of a distant country (for example a US state or England)
  when neither party's business is based there. A small business would need foreign lawyers, and
  travel, even to defend a weak claim.
- **Medium:** the discloser's home law when the receiver is the smaller party, with exclusive courts
  there; workable between Malaysia and Singapore, harder further away.
- **Medium:** the law of one place but the courts of another, which multiplies cost.
- **Low:** no governing law stated; ask for one to avoid an argument later.

## Suggested ask
"Please change the governing law to Malaysian (or Singapore) law, with the courts of Kuala Lumpur
(or Singapore), since both parties do business in this region."

title: Dispute resolution: courts, mediation or arbitration (NDA)
plain: How a disagreement gets settled: talking first, then a mediator, then a court or an arbitrator (a private judge whose decision is binding).
text:
clause_type: `dispute_resolution` · contract_type: `nda`

## In plain words
How a disagreement gets settled: talking first, then a mediator, then a court or an arbitrator
(a private judge whose decision is binding).

## What balanced looks like
- A short step of **good-faith talks** between senior people, for example 14 to 30 days.
- Then **courts** in the governing-law country, or **arbitration** in the region: the Asian
  International Arbitration Centre (**AIAC**, Kuala Lumpur) or the Singapore International
  Arbitration Centre (**SIAC**). Mediation centres in both cities are a cheaper first step.
- A single arbitrator for small claims, to keep cost down.
- Either side may still go to court for an urgent injunction.
- Each side pays its own costs unless the tribunal or court decides otherwise.

## Red flags
- **High:** arbitration or courts in a distant city with rules that make even a small claim cost more
  than it is worth.
- **Medium:** only one side may choose between court and arbitration.
- **Medium:** the receiver must pay the discloser's legal costs whatever the outcome.
- **Medium:** the receiver waives its right to go to court or to appeal, while the discloser keeps it.
- **Low:** no dispute clause at all; the courts of the governing-law country then apply by default.

## Suggested ask
"Please provide for talks first, then mediation or arbitration in Kuala Lumpur (AIAC) or Singapore
(SIAC) with one arbitrator, and let each party bear its own costs."

title: Assignment: passing the contract to someone else (NDA)
plain: Whether a party may transfer its rights or duties under the NDA to another company, for example a buyer of its business.
text:
clause_type: `assignment` · contract_type: `nda`

## In plain words
Whether a party may transfer its rights or duties under the NDA to another company, for example a
buyer of its business.

## What balanced looks like
- **Neither side** may assign without the other's written consent.
- **Exception:** either side may assign to a company that takes over all or most of its business in a
  merger or sale, without needing consent.
- Consent is not to be unreasonably withheld.

## Red flags
- **Medium:** the discloser may assign to anyone, including a competitor of the receiver, while the
  receiver may never assign.
- **Medium:** the discloser may share the receiver's information across its whole group of companies
  without the same duties applying to each of them.
- **Low:** no assignment clause; usually harmless in an NDA.

## Suggested ask
"Please make the assignment rule mutual: no assignment without consent, except to a successor in a
merger or sale of the business."

title: Term: how long the agreement runs (service agreement)
plain: The start date, the first fixed period (the "initial term") and what happens at the end of it. Renewal is covered separately in `auto_renewal.md`.
text:
clause_type: `term` · contract_type: `service_agreement`

## In plain words
The start date, the first fixed period (the "initial term") and what happens at the end of it.
Renewal is covered separately in `auto_renewal.md`.

## What balanced looks like
- An initial term of **12 months** for subscriptions and ongoing services; up to **24-36 months** only
  when the customer gets a real price discount in return.
- Project work ends when the project is delivered and accepted, or on a stated end date.
- The start date is clear, and paid service starts only when the service is actually available
  ("go-live"), not on signature months earlier.
- Clauses that should outlive the contract (confidentiality, payment of amounts already due,
  liability) are listed as surviving.

## Red flags
- **High:** a long initial term (3 years or more) that the customer cannot leave early, with all fees
  for the whole term payable even if the service is poor.
- **Medium:** fees start on signature although set-up takes months.
- **Medium:** the vendor may extend the term on its own by issuing a new order or "service schedule".
- **Low:** no stated end date for project work; ask for one.

## Suggested ask
"Please set a 12-month initial term starting on go-live, and confirm the customer may end it early
as set out in the termination clause."

title: Auto-renewal and price increases on renewal (service agreement)
plain: An auto-renewal clause rolls the contract into a new period unless someone gives notice in time. It is convenient, but a long notice window or a long renewal period can lock a business in by accident. Price rises are covered in `payment.md`; a rise tied to renewal is flagged here as well.
text:
clause_type: `auto_renewal` · contract_type: `service_agreement`

## In plain words
An auto-renewal clause rolls the contract into a new period unless someone gives notice in time. It
is convenient, but a long notice window or a long renewal period can lock a business in by accident.
Price rises are covered in `payment.md`; a rise tied to renewal is flagged here as well.

## What balanced looks like
- Renewal for **the same or a shorter period**, usually 12 months or month-to-month.
- **Notice to stop renewal of 30 days** before the end date (60 days at most).
- The vendor **sends a reminder** 30-60 days before the notice deadline.
- After renewal, the customer may still leave on reasonable notice, or renewal is month-to-month.
- Any price change on renewal is announced at least 60 days ahead and capped (see `payment.md`).

## Red flags
- **High:** a notice window of **90 days or more**, especially combined with a renewal period longer
  than the original term (for example 24 months).
- **High:** renewal plus an automatic price increase well above inflation.
- **Medium:** notice must be given by a special method (registered post only, a named person only)
  that is easy to get wrong.
- **Medium:** only the vendor may decide not to renew.
- **Low:** 60-day notice window with a reminder; acceptable but worth diarising.

## Suggested ask
"Please change renewal to 12-month periods with 30 days' notice to stop renewal, and have the vendor
send a written reminder 60 days before the renewal date."
