title: Termination: how either side can end the agreement (service agreement)
plain: When and how the contract can be ended before its natural end, and what each side owes afterwards.
text:
clause_type: `termination` · contract_type: `service_agreement`

## In plain words
When and how the contract can be ended before its natural end, and what each side owes afterwards.

## What balanced looks like
- **For cause, both sides:** either side may end it if the other commits a serious breach and does
  not fix it within **30 days** of written notice, or becomes insolvent.
- **For convenience:** the customer (and often both sides) may end it without a reason on **30 to 90
  days'** notice, paying for work done and committed costs up to that date.
- **The same notice periods for both sides**, or a longer period for the vendor (so the customer has
  time to switch).
- **Exit help:** the customer gets its data back in a usable format within about 30 days, and
  reasonable transition help at normal rates.
- Prepaid fees for services not yet delivered are refunded when the vendor is at fault.

## Red flags
- **High:** the customer may not end early for any reason, or must pay all remaining fees for the
  whole term as an "early termination fee".
- **Medium:** the vendor may end on very short notice (for example 7 days) without cause, while the
  customer needs months.
- **Medium:** no cure period: one minor late payment lets the vendor end the contract at once.
- **Medium:** the customer's data is deleted on termination with no export window.
- **Low:** no exit-assistance wording; ask for a data export at minimum.

## Suggested ask
"Please give both parties the same notice period, allow 30 days to fix a breach, and add a 30-day
window to export our data on termination."

title: Payment, late interest and price increases (service agreement)
plain: How much is paid, when, what happens if payment is late, and whether the vendor may raise prices.
text:
clause_type: `payment` · contract_type: `service_agreement`

## In plain words
How much is paid, when, what happens if payment is late, and whether the vendor may raise prices.

## What balanced looks like
- **Payment within 30 days** of a correct invoice (30-60 days is common in Malaysia and Singapore).
- Prices stated **excluding tax**, with Malaysian service tax (SST) or Singapore GST added where it
  applies.
- **Disputed invoices:** the customer may hold back the disputed part in good faith while paying the
  rest, and both sides try to resolve it quickly.
- **Late interest** at a modest rate, roughly **0.5% to 1% a month** (or a fixed annual rate around
  5-8%), only after a reminder.
- **Suspension** for non-payment only after written notice and a further 14-30 days.
- **Price increases** no more than once a year, with **at least 60 days' notice**, capped at
  inflation or a fixed low figure (for example 3-5%), and a right to leave if the customer refuses.

## Red flags
- **High:** an automatic increase of **10% or more every year**, or an increase "at the vendor's
  discretion" with no cap.
- **Medium:** payment within 7 or 14 days.
- **Medium:** late interest of 2% a month or more, or interest plus collection fees plus suspension.
- **Medium:** the customer must pay in full even when it disputes the invoice.
- **Low:** fees payable annually in advance; common for software, but check refund terms.

## Suggested ask
"Please set payment at 30 days from invoice, late interest at no more than 1% a month, and cap
any annual price increase at 5% with 60 days' written notice."

title: Limitation of liability: the most either side can be made to pay (service agreement)
plain: A liability cap sets the maximum amount one side can be made to pay the other if things go wrong. An exclusion lists kinds of loss that cannot be claimed at all, such as lost profits.
text:
clause_type: `liability` · contract_type: `service_agreement`

## In plain words
A liability cap sets the maximum amount one side can be made to pay the other if things go wrong.
An exclusion lists kinds of loss that cannot be claimed at all, such as lost profits.

## What balanced looks like
- **Mutual cap**: the same cap for both sides, usually **the fees paid or payable in the 12 months**
  before the claim.
- **Mutual exclusion** of indirect losses (lost profits, lost business, loss of reputation) for both
  sides.
- **Carve-outs from the cap** (amounts that stay uncapped or have a higher cap) apply to both sides
  equally: fraud, death or personal injury caused by negligence, breach of confidentiality, data
  protection breaches (often a higher "super-cap", such as 2-3 times annual fees), and the vendor's
  IP infringement indemnity.
- The customer's obligation to pay fees for services received is not limited by the cap.

## Red flags
- **High:** the vendor's cap is tiny, for example **one month's fees** or a fixed small sum, so even
  a serious failure costs the vendor almost nothing.
- **High:** the customer's liability is **uncapped** while the vendor's is capped: a one-sided cap.
- **High:** the vendor excludes liability for data loss or security breaches entirely.
- **Medium:** a cap of 3-6 months' fees, or a cap that applies only to the vendor's side.
- **Medium:** the indirect-loss exclusion protects only the vendor.
- **Low:** a 12-month mutual cap with a lower carve-out list; usually acceptable.

## Suggested ask
"Please make the limitation of liability mutual, set the cap at the fees paid in the previous 12
months for both parties, and apply the same exclusions and carve-outs to both."

title: Indemnity: promising to cover the other side's losses (service agreement)
plain: An indemnity is a promise to pay the other side's losses and legal costs if a particular thing happens, usually a claim brought by an outsider. It can be much wider than ordinary damages, so its scope matters.
text:
clause_type: `indemnity` · contract_type: `service_agreement`

## In plain words
An indemnity is a promise to pay the other side's losses and legal costs if a particular thing
happens, usually a claim brought by an outsider. It can be much wider than ordinary damages, so its
scope matters.

## What balanced looks like
- **Vendor indemnifies the customer** if a third party claims the vendor's service or deliverables
  infringe their IP (copyright, patent, trade mark). This is the most common indemnity.
- **Customer indemnifies the vendor** only if a third party claims that content or data the customer
  supplied infringes their rights or breaks the law.
- Indemnities cover **third-party claims**, not every loss between the two parties.
- The protected side must **tell the other promptly**, let it **control the defence**, and cooperate.
- Losses caused by the protected side's own negligence or breach are excluded.
- Indemnity amounts are capped like other liability, or sit under an agreed higher cap.

## Red flags
- **High:** the customer indemnifies the vendor against "any and all" losses "arising out of or in
  connection with" the agreement, even those caused by the vendor's own negligence.
- **High:** a one-way indemnity from the customer only, with no IP indemnity from the vendor.
- **Medium:** the indemnity covers the vendor's own losses (not only third-party claims) and is
  uncapped.
- **Medium:** no duty to notify, and no right for the indemnifying side to control the defence.

## Suggested ask
"Please limit the customer's indemnity to third-party claims caused by our own data or breach,
exclude losses caused by the vendor's negligence, and add the vendor's standard IP infringement
indemnity."

title: Ownership of work product and IP (service agreement)
plain: Who owns what is created under the contract. ("IP", intellectual property, covers software code, designs, documents, data models and brands.)
text:
clause_type: `ip_ownership` · contract_type: `service_agreement`

## In plain words
Who owns what is created under the contract. ("IP", intellectual property, covers software code,
designs, documents, data models and brands.)

## What balanced looks like
- **Custom deliverables belong to the customer** once paid for: work made specifically for the
  customer (a custom app, a design, a report) transfers to the customer on payment.
- **The vendor keeps its existing tools and platform** ("background IP") and general know-how, and
  gives the customer a **licence** (permission) to use whatever is built into the deliverables, for as
  long as the customer uses them.
- **The customer keeps all its own data** and content. The vendor may use it only to provide the
  service.
- Source code for custom software is handed over, or held in escrow, if the customer will need to
  maintain it.

## Red flags
- **High:** the vendor owns custom work the customer paid to have built, and the customer gets only a
  licence that ends when the contract ends.
- **High:** the vendor owns or may freely reuse the customer's data, or anything "derived" from it.
- **Medium:** ownership passes only after every fee under the whole agreement is paid, not per
  deliverable.
- **Medium:** no source code delivery for custom software the customer depends on.
- **Low:** the vendor may reuse general know-how and non-customer-specific components; normal.

## Suggested ask
"Please confirm that all deliverables created specifically for us belong to us on payment, with a
continuing licence to any vendor tools built into them, and that our data remains ours."

title: Warranties: what the vendor promises about the service (service agreement)
plain: A warranty is a promise about quality: that the service will be done properly and the software will work as described. It also says what the customer gets if the promise is broken.
text:
clause_type: `warranty` · contract_type: `service_agreement`

## In plain words
A warranty is a promise about quality: that the service will be done properly and the software will
work as described. It also says what the customer gets if the promise is broken.

## What balanced looks like
- Services performed **with reasonable skill and care**, by suitably qualified people, in line with
  good industry practice.
- Deliverables and software **match the agreed specification** or documentation.
- **A defects period** of about **90 days** after acceptance in which the vendor fixes defects free.
- **Service levels** for hosted services (for example 99.5% monthly availability) with service
  credits if missed, and a right to end the contract after repeated failures.
- Vendor confirms it has the rights to provide the service and complies with applicable law.
- Disclaimers of other implied promises are acceptable once the above are given.

## Red flags
- **High:** everything provided "as is" with no promise of any kind, for a paid service.
- **Medium:** the only remedy is a small service credit, even for a long outage.
- **Medium:** defects must be reported within a few days, or the warranty is lost.
- **Medium:** no acceptance testing before the customer must pay in full.
- **Low:** a 30-day defects period instead of 90; worth asking to extend.

## Suggested ask
"Please add a warranty that services are performed with reasonable skill and care and match the
specification, with free fixes for defects reported within 90 days of acceptance."

title: Confidentiality (service agreement)
plain: Both sides will see each other's business information while the service runs. This clause keeps it secret and limits how it is used.
text:
clause_type: `confidentiality` · contract_type: `service_agreement`

## In plain words
Both sides will see each other's business information while the service runs. This clause keeps it
secret and limits how it is used.

## What balanced looks like
- **Mutual** obligations.
- Confidential information is what is marked, or obviously, confidential, and includes the
  customer's data and the contract's pricing.
- Use only to perform the agreement; share only with staff and subcontractors who need it and are
  bound by similar duties.
- The standard exceptions: public information, already known, received lawfully from a third party,
  independently developed, and disclosure required by law with prior notice where allowed.
- Lasts for the contract plus **2 to 5 years**, and for trade secrets and personal data as long as
  they remain so.

## Red flags
- **High:** only the customer is bound, while the vendor holds the customer's business data with no
  duty of secrecy.
- **Medium:** the vendor may publicise the customer as a reference, or publish case studies, without
  consent.
- **Medium:** no exceptions, or no right to disclose where the law requires.
- **Low:** a 1-year survival period; short, but not dangerous for ordinary information.

## Suggested ask
"Please make the confidentiality obligations mutual, with the standard exceptions, lasting at least
three years after the agreement ends, and require our consent before naming us publicly."

title: Personal data protection (service agreement)
plain: When a vendor handles personal data (about the customer's staff, patients or customers) on the customer's behalf, the contract should say how the vendor keeps it safe. Malaysia and Singapore each have a Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), and in both the customer usually stays responsible for what its vendors do with the data.
text:
clause_type: `data_protection` · contract_type: `service_agreement`

## In plain words
When a vendor handles personal data (about the customer's staff, patients or customers) on the
customer's behalf, the contract should say how the vendor keeps it safe. Malaysia and Singapore each
have a Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), and in both the customer usually stays responsible for
what its vendors do with the data.

## What balanced looks like
- The vendor processes personal data **only on the customer's instructions** and only to provide the
  service.
- **Reasonable security** measures, described or referenced (access control, encryption, staff
  training).
- **Breach notice** to the customer **without undue delay**, with a fixed outer limit such as 24-72
  hours after discovery, so the customer can meet its own reporting duties.
- **Subcontractors** only with notice to the customer and on the same terms.
- **Transfers outside Malaysia or Singapore** only with adequate protection.
- **Return or deletion** of personal data at the end, with written confirmation.
- Help with requests from individuals to access or correct their data.
- Liability for data breaches is not excluded; often under a higher, mutual "super-cap".

## Red flags
- **High:** no data protection clause at all when the service handles personal data.
- **High:** the vendor may use the personal data for its own purposes (marketing, training products,
  selling insights).
- **Medium:** breach notice only "as soon as practicable" with no outer limit, or none at all.
- **Medium:** data may be stored or transferred anywhere without notice.
- **Low:** security described only in general terms; ask for a summary of measures.

## Suggested ask
"Please add a data protection clause: processing only on our instructions, reasonable security,
breach notice within 48 hours, approved subcontractors, and return or deletion of data at the end."

title: Governing law: which country's law applies (service agreement)
plain: Which country's law is used to read the contract, and where a case would be heard. A distant law or court makes any dispute slower and more expensive for the smaller side.
text:
clause_type: `governing_law` · contract_type: `service_agreement`

## In plain words
Which country's law is used to read the contract, and where a case would be heard. A distant law or
court makes any dispute slower and more expensive for the smaller side.

## What balanced looks like
- The law of the country where the **customer** receives the service, or where both sides are based.
- Malaysian law with Kuala Lumpur courts, or Singapore law with Singapore courts, for a contract
  between companies in these two countries.
- The courts named match the law chosen.
- Non-exclusive jurisdiction, or arbitration in the region (see `dispute_resolution.md`).

## Red flags
- **High:** the law and exclusive courts of a country where neither party operates.
- **Medium:** the vendor's home law and exclusive courts when the vendor is much larger and abroad.
- **Medium:** a mismatch: one country's law but another country's courts.
- **Low:** no governing law clause.

## Suggested ask
"Please make the agreement subject to Malaysian law (or Singapore law) and the courts of Kuala
Lumpur (or Singapore), where both parties operate."

title: Dispute resolution (service agreement)
plain: The steps for settling a disagreement before it becomes a costly case.
text:
clause_type: `dispute_resolution` · contract_type: `service_agreement`

## In plain words
The steps for settling a disagreement before it becomes a costly case.

## What balanced looks like
- **Escalation:** the project managers talk first, then senior managers, within fixed short periods
  (for example 10 business days each).
- **Mediation** at a regional centre (for example the AIAC in Kuala Lumpur or the Singapore
  International Mediation Centre) if talks fail; it is quick and cheap.
- Then **courts** of the governing-law country, or **arbitration** at the AIAC or SIAC with one
  arbitrator for smaller disputes.
- **Service continues** during a dispute; the vendor may not suspend while a good-faith dispute is
  being worked through, provided undisputed amounts are paid.
- Either side may seek urgent relief from a court at any time.

## Red flags
- **High:** the vendor may suspend the whole service during any dispute.
- **High:** arbitration in a distant city with three arbitrators for any claim, making small claims
  pointless.
- **Medium:** only the vendor may start court proceedings; the customer must arbitrate.
- **Medium:** the losing side always pays the winner's costs on a full indemnity basis, which deters
  the smaller side from raising genuine complaints.
- **Low:** no escalation step; ask for one.

## Suggested ask
"Please add an escalation and mediation step before any proceedings, keep the service running
during a good-faith dispute, and use courts or arbitration in Kuala Lumpur or Singapore."
